name: L-theanine

lead: L-theanine is an amino acid found mainly in tea leaves, sold for relaxation, focus and sleep, often alongside caffeine. Users treat the calm and better rest as a base for skin, mood and a more composed presentation.

It resembles glutamate and weakly interacts with glutamate receptors in lab studies. Small human studies report reduced stress responses and effects on cognition and mood, while EFSA found insufficient support for claims on cognition, stress and sleep, and a 2025 review criticized the rigor of much of the literature.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or powder, with coffee for smoother focus or in the evening for winding down. It is a common part of sleep and calm stacks.
Safety data are limited, and a German agency warned about effects with sedatives. It is sold over the counter in the US and is GRAS up to 250 mg per serving in foods.

angle.text: Users take this tea amino acid to relax, focus and sleep, treating calm and rest as a base for skin and looks. Small studies report reduced stress responses; its link to appearance has not been tested.

lead: L-theanine is a non-proteinogenic amino acid found mainly in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis) and sold as a supplement for relaxation, focus and sleep, often alongside caffeine [1]. It was identified in green tea in 1949 and isolated from gyokuro leaves in 1950 [1].

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheap way to calm anxiety, improve focus with coffee and sleep better, which proponents tie to better skin, mood and presentation. Small human studies report reduced stress responses and effects on cognition and mood, but regulators and reviews describe the evidence as mixed [1][2][3].

The European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence for claims that theanine improves cognition, reduces stress or supports sleep, and a 2025 review criticized the rigor of much of the literature [1].
infobox: OTC supplement; FDA GRAS in foods up to 250 mg per serving [1]

paras: Theanine makes up about 1 percent of the dry weight of black, green and white tea, and shaded teas such as matcha and gyokuro contain more [1]. It contributes to the umami taste of Japanese green tea [4]. Commercial products may contain some D-form because heat and pH can convert the natural L-form [1].

After oral intake it is absorbed in the small intestine and broken down to glutamate and ethylamine [1]. It weakly binds glutamate receptors, blocking AMPA and kainate and partially activating NMDA receptors in lab work [1]. A small study found an EEG alpha-wave effect for GABA but compared it with theanine in the same experiment [5].

A 2007 study of twelve volunteers found that L-theanine reduced psychological and physiological stress responses to a mental arithmetic task [6]. A 2008 study examined theanine, caffeine and their combination on cognition and mood [7]. A 2017 review covered its metabolism, health effects and safety [2]. In 2011 the EFSA found claims for cognition, stress and sleep unsupported, while a 2020 review suggested 200-400 mg daily might reduce stress during acute stress but judged evidence insufficient for medical use [1].

Safety data are limited. In 2003 Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment objected to adding isolated theanine to drinks, warning of possible effects on psychomotor skills and sedatives [1]. In the US it is sold as a supplement and the FDA considers it generally recognized as safe in foods up to 250 mg per serving; Japan approved its food use in 1964 [1].

Registered studies include a phase 2 trial in boys with ADHD (n=100) [8], a trial of caffeine and theanine on cerebral blood flow, cognition and mood [9], a phase 3 trial in schizophrenia (n=60) [10], and studies in athletes and stressed adults [11]. Published findings include the 2007 stress study [6] and the 2008 cognition study [7]. Reviews in 2024 reported possible benefit over placebo for anxiety, ADHD and schizophrenia symptoms, while a 2025 review criticized unreliable trials [1].
